title: Penguin Body Mass by Species: R
text:
Topic:
How does body mass vary among the three penguin species in the Palmer Penguins dataset? I will check missing values, calculate a summary for each species, and plot the measurements.
Data: Palmer Penguins, collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Antarctica LTER Program. Licence: CC0.

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

penguins |> count(species)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species       n
  <fct>     <int>
1 Adelie      152
2 Chinstrap    68
3 Gentoo      124


The dataset contains three species. And beofre comparing body mass, I will check how many measurements are missing.

penguins |>
  summarise(
    total_rows = n(),
    missing_body_mass = sum(is.na(body_mass_g))
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  total_rows missing_body_mass
       <int>             <int>
1        344                 2

mass_summary <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    penguins = n(),
    mean_mass_g = round(mean(body_mass_g), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

mass_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  species   penguins mean_mass_g
  <fct>        <int>       <dbl>
1 Adelie         151       3701.
2 Chinstrap       68       3733.
3 Gentoo         123       5076 


The table compares the number of recorded body masses and their mean for each species. I excluded missing body mass values from the calculation.

ggplot(
  penguins |> filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)),
  aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(fill = "none")







Figure 1: Body mass measurements by penguin species.





The plot shows both the differences between species and the variation within each species. The summary table identifies which species has the highest mean; the boxplots show that individual penguins also vary in mass.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation day on campus.



My First Weeks in MDS
My first week in the MDS program have been exciting and busy. Orientation was a great opportunity to meet my classmates and learn more about the program. There was a lot of new information to take in, but I was excited to start this new chapter and get to know the people I will be studying with over the next year.
The first week of classes was definitely more intense than I expected. We started working with Python, R, Git, GitHub, and the command line very quickly. Coming from a Statistics background at the University of Toronto, I was familiar with R and statistical concepts, but some of the programming tools and workflows were new to me. I was especially surprised by how quickly we moved from learning concepts to actually using them in worksheets and labs.
Now that I have made it through the first two weeks, almost? I am starting to feel more comfortable with the pace and the tools we use. There is still a lot to learn, and sometimes it can feel overwhelming, but I am enjoying the challenge. I am looking forward to improving my programming skills, learning more about data science, and seeing how much I will grow throughout the MDS program.

title: Penguin Body Mass by Species: Python
text:
How does body mass vary among the three penguin species in the Palmer Penguins dataset? I will repeat the R analysis in Python: check missing values, calculate species means, and make a plot.
Data: Palmer Penguins, collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Antarctica LTER Program. Licence: CC0.

from palmerpenguins import load_penguins
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

penguins = load_penguins()
print(penguins["species"].value_counts())

species
Adelie       152
Gentoo       124
Chinstrap     68
Name: count, dtype: int64


The dataset contains three species. I check for missing body mass values before calculating the averages.

print("Total rows:", len(penguins))
print("Missing body masses:", penguins["body_mass_g"].isna().sum())

mass_data = penguins.dropna(subset=["body_mass_g"])
mass_summary = (
    mass_data.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"]
    .agg(penguins="count", mean_mass_g="mean")
    .round(1)
)
print(mass_summary)

Total rows: 344
Missing body masses: 2
           penguins  mean_mass_g
species                         
Adelie          151       3700.7
Chinstrap        68       3733.1
Gentoo          123       5076.0


The table reports how many penguins have a body mass measurement in each species and their mean body mass. Rows with missing body mass were excluded.

species = sorted(mass_data["species"].unique())
values = [
    mass_data.loc[mass_data["species"] == name, "body_mass_g"]
    for name in species
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.boxplot(values, tick_labels=species)
ax.set_xlabel("Species")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Body mass measurements by penguin species.





The plot shows how body mass differs across species, as well as variation among penguins of the same species. Compare the table and plot with the R post: both analyses use the same measurements and exclude missing body mass values.
